title: Culture Doesn’t Just Happen
author: Katie Martin
summary: Katie Martin uses a Padres playoff game at Petco Park to argue that culture is built through deliberate, repeated shared experiences rather than assumed from good intentions. Even a stadium full of devoted fans is prompted with scoreboard cues, music, videos and traditions such as "Sweet Caroline" at Fenway, and many of those rituals began small before leaders noticed and amplified them. She applies the lesson to schools, where a Portrait of a Learner on posters names aspirations like collaboration and agency but cannot by itself create the culture to realize them. Culture grows from what people repeatedly experience, practice, notice and celebrate, and that must include the adults, who need symmetry between what is promised to students and what staff actually live. Leaders should therefore attend to the rhythms and rituals of meetings, time, professional learning and storytelling.
points: Even highly invested people benefit from deliberate cues and rituals, so schools cannot assume that caring educators and families will self-organize into a shared culture.
Rituals often begin small, as an observed behavior that someone notices, amplifies and repeats until it becomes part of identity.
A Portrait of a Learner is a North Star, not a culture: values only become culture when people repeatedly experience them in how time, decisions and recognition work.
Adults need symmetry with students, because teachers cannot foster agency or collaboration while working in compliance-driven, isolated systems.
Leaders should audit the rhythms of the system (meeting design, time allocation, professional learning, stories told, what is celebrated) as the school equivalent of the stadium's scoreboard prompts.
quotes: Nobody in the Padres organization seemed to be thinking, These fans bought tickets. They know why they’re here. If they really care, they’ll figure it out. They were actively creating the conditions for us to show up as a community.
The specific ritual isn’t the point. The repetition is. The shared experience is. The meaning people attach to it is.
These places remind us that culture is not simply something a group of people has. Culture is something people create together, experience together, and reinforce over time.
A Portrait of a Learner can articulate what we value. It can give us a North Star. But it cannot create the culture required to bring those aspirations to life.
Culture is built through what people repeatedly experience, practice, notice, celebrate, and reinforce.

We cannot ask educators to create classrooms characterized by agency while they work in systems defined by compliance. We cannot expect teachers to foster collaboration if their own schedules isolate them from colleagues.
There has to be symmetry between what we say we want for young people and what the adults in the system experience.

The work of culture isn’t convincing people to care. It’s intentionally creating the experiences, rituals, structures, and reminders that help all of us turn what we care about into how we show up—again and again and again.
